--- title: "Reporting a model" description: "A report lets a reader re-run an analysis and use its model within its limits. The raw data, the code, the seeds and the software versions make the numbers repeat, and a model card, written from the code, says what the model is, how well it predicts and where it holds." order: 5 categories: [reproducibility, interpretation] --- {{< new-terms >}} ## A report lets others re-run a model and use it A fitted model reaches two kinds of reader. One wants to check the numbers: to run the same code on the same data and see the same results. The other wants to use the predictions, and needs to know what the model was built for and where it can be trusted. This page covers both: the habits that let anyone re-run an analysis, and a short, fixed set of entries, the model card, that goes with the model wherever its predictions are used. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the data on this page The coastal survey used here is **simulated**, not a real survey. That is deliberate: because we wrote the generating process (`R/make-example-data.R`), we know the true relationships and can show whether a model recovers them. No real survey is being misrepresented, and the figures are not results about any real species. See `data/README.md` for what is built into it. ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the Python tabs Most code blocks on this page have an **R** and a **Python** tab, and picking one switches the whole page. Both run when the site is built, and each tab shows its own output. The Python tab is the scikit-learn equivalent of the R; the figures come from R throughout, and a few steps with no scikit-learn counterpart have no Python tab, which is itself worth noticing. Expect the **numbers to differ slightly** where randomness is involved: R and Python draw their random splits from different generators, so the split is not the same one. The conclusions are. ::: ## A re-runnable analysis keeps four things An analysis is **reproducible** when someone else, given the same data and the same code, gets the same numbers. A reader can then check a result, and you can return to your own analysis a year later and pick up where you left off. Four things make it so. ::: {.diagram} ![Four things a re-run needs: the raw data, kept as collected; every step in code, from the raw file to the score; a seed above each random draw; and the versions of the software. With all four, anyone can re-run the analysis and get the same numbers.](img/re-run.svg){fig-alt="Four cards. The raw data, kept as collected: the file as it came in, never edited by hand, drawn as a locked table. Every step in code, in scripts: from the raw file to the score, cleaning, fitting and scoring, drawn as four boxes, raw, clean, model and score, joined by arrows. A seed above each draw, for random choices: set just before the draw it is for, so each step gets the same draws every run, drawn as two runs from seed 1 giving the same three numbers. The software versions, in a lockfile: each package and its version, so a reader can install the same ones, drawn as a table of packages A, B and C with their versions. A note says that with all four anyone can re-run the analysis and get the same numbers."} ::: This course keeps all four. The survey's raw file, `data/coastal-survey-raw.csv`, is never edited; `load_coastal_survey_clean()` turns it into the clean survey in code, dropping duplicate rows, turning missing-value codes into gaps, correcting depth errors and merging the spellings of the seabed. `renv.lock` records the version of every R package, and `renv::restore()` installs the same versions; in Python, `pip freeze > requirements.txt` records them. And every number in the text of these pages is computed by the page's own code, not typed, so the text cannot quote a number the code no longer gives. A report written as a Quarto or R Markdown document works the same way. The seed needs the most care. A split, a random forest and a shuffle all draw from a random number generator, and a **seed** sets where its sequence of numbers starts. It does not fix which step gets which number. An extra draw before the split, even one hidden inside another function, shifts every draw after it, and the worked example shows one. ## A model card says what a model is for and where it holds A **model card** is a short document that travels with a model. The idea comes from machine learning in general (Mitchell and colleagues, 2019), and the entries suit a model of survey data well: | Entry | Says | Comes from | | --- | --- | --- | | Model | The method, its package and version, and its settings | The code | | Intended use | What the predictions are for, and what they are not for | The study's aim | | Data | Where the records come from, how many stations and sites, and how they were caught | [Exploring and cleaning the data](../02-marine-data/exploring-and-cleaning.qmd) | | Inputs | What the model predicts from, and how gaps were filled | The recipe | | Score | Its typical miss on sites it never saw | [The test sites](../02-marine-data/splitting-data.qmd) | | What it relies on | The inputs it uses most, and the shape of its strongest effect | [Feature importance](feature-importance.qmd), [Partial effects](partial-effects.qmd) | | Where it holds | The range of each input it was fitted to | The training stations | | Limits | What the predictions cannot say | [Uneven sampling and extrapolation](../06-assumptions-limitations/sampling-and-extrapolation.qmd) | ::: {.diagram} ![A model card in three parts: what the model is, how well it predicts on sites it never saw, and where it holds.](img/model-card.svg){fig-alt="Three cards. What the model is, model, data and inputs: the method, its settings, the data and how they were collected, drawn as a form with lines for model, data and inputs. How well it predicts, score on new sites: its typical miss on sites it never saw, in the outcome's units, drawn as six stations at held-out sites, each with a predicted count, a recorded count and the miss between them. Where it holds, range and intended use: the range of the inputs it was fitted to and the uses it was built for, drawn as stations inside a shaded band along an input such as temperature, with question marks on either side. A note says that a model card travels with the model, so its users know what it can and cannot do."} ::: The card is a record of what has already been measured, not a new analysis. Each entry is a sentence or two, and each number in it comes from the code, as the worked example shows. ## Worked example The random forest of the earlier pages in this section predicts abundance from depth, temperature, chlorophyll, salinity, substrate and season. It is fitted to the training sites of the same split and scored on its test sites. The example first breaks a seed with a hidden draw, then writes the forest's model card from the code. ### Preparing the data ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} survey <- load_coastal_survey_clean() inputs <- c("depth_m", "temperature_c", "chlorophyll_mg_m3", "salinity_psu", "substrate", "season") split <- group_initial_split(survey, group = site_id, prop = 0.75) train <- training(split) test <- testing(split) forest_recipe <- recipe(reformulate(inputs, "abundance"), data = train) |> step_impute_median(all_numeric_predictors()) forest_model <- rand_forest(trees = 500) |> set_engine("ranger", seed = 123) |> set_mode("regression") forest <- workflow(forest_recipe, forest_model) |> fit(train) ``` ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} import numpy as np import pandas as pd from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestRegressor from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer from sklearn.inspection import partial_dependence, permutation_importance from sklearn.metrics import root_mean_squared_error from sklearn.model_selection import GroupShuffleSplit from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder from mlbasic_data import load_coastal_survey_clean survey = load_coastal_survey_clean() sites = survey["site_id"] grouper = GroupShuffleSplit(n_splits=1, train_size=0.75, random_state=123) train_rows, test_rows = next(grouper.split(survey, groups=sites)) train = survey.iloc[train_rows].reset_index(drop=True) test = survey.iloc[test_rows].reset_index(drop=True) numeric = ["depth_m", "temperature_c", "chlorophyll_mg_m3", "salinity_psu"] categorical = ["substrate", "season"] inputs = numeric + categorical recipe = ColumnTransformer( [("numeric", SimpleImputer(strategy="median"), numeric), ("categorical", OneHotEncoder(drop="first", sparse_output=False), categorical)]) # max_features and min_samples_leaf match ranger's defaults model = RandomForestRegressor(n_estimators=500, max_features="sqrt", min_samples_leaf=5, random_state=123) forest = Pipeline([("recipe", recipe), ("model", model)]).fit( train[inputs], train["abundance"]) ``` ::: ::: ### A hidden draw moves a seeded split The split is drawn twice from the same seed. The second time, a recipe is built between the seed and the split. In R, `recipe()` and each `step_*()` draw a random ID, so the recipe takes numbers from the sequence that the split would otherwise have used. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(123) first <- group_initial_split(survey, group = site_id, prop = 0.75) set.seed(123) depth_recipe <- recipe(abundance ~ depth_m, data = survey) |> step_impute_median(all_numeric_predictors()) # draws a random ID second <- group_initial_split(survey, group = site_id, prop = 0.75) test_sites <- \(split) unique(testing(split)$site_id) shared <- length(intersect(test_sites(first), test_sites(second))) tibble(Run = c("Seed, then split", "Seed, recipe, then split"), `Test sites` = c(length(test_sites(first)), length(test_sites(second))), `Shared with the first run` = c(length(test_sites(first)), shared)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|Run | Test sites| Shared with the first run| |:------------------------|----------:|-------------------------:| |Seed, then split | 40| 40| |Seed, recipe, then split | 36| 23|
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} # without its own random_state, a function draws from numpy's global # generator, which np.random.seed() sets as set.seed() does in R def unseeded_split(): grouper = GroupShuffleSplit(n_splits=1, train_size=0.75) return next(grouper.split(survey, groups=sites)) np.random.seed(123) first = unseeded_split() np.random.seed(123) extra = np.random.permutation(10) # one extra draw, as in another function second = unseeded_split() def test_sites(split): return set(sites.iloc[split[1]]) pd.DataFrame({ "Run": ["Seed, then split", "Seed, extra draw, then split"], "Test sites": [len(test_sites(first)), len(test_sites(second))], "Shared with the first run": [ len(test_sites(first)), len(test_sites(first) & test_sites(second))], }) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | Run | Test sites | Shared with the first run | |:-----------------------------|-------------:|----------------------------:| | Seed, then split | 40 | 40 | | Seed, extra draw, then split | 40 | 22 | ::: ::: ::: Both runs set the same seed, yet only 23 of the first run's 40 test sites are among the second run's 36, and nothing warned. The first run is the split this section's pages use; the second would have given every page different numbers. Setting the seed on the line above the draw it is for, as these pages do, keeps each draw where it was. In scikit-learn, give each function its own `random_state`; its draws then do not depend on anything that ran before it. ### The model card is written from the code Every number the card needs is computed here: the forest's typical miss on the test sites, how far shuffling each input raises it, the temperature at which the partial dependence peaks, and the range of depth and temperature over the training stations. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} test_rmse <- rmse_vec(test$abundance, predict(forest, test)$.pred) # the rise in test RMSE when an input is shuffled, as in Feature importance error <- \(d) rmse_vec(d$abundance, predict(forest, d)$.pred) importance <- map(inputs, \(input) { rises <- map_dbl(1:20, \(i) { shuffled <- test shuffled[[input]] <- sample(shuffled[[input]]) error(shuffled) - test_rmse }) tibble(input, rise = mean(rises)) }) |> list_rbind() |> arrange(desc(rise)) # the partial dependence on temperature, as in Partial effects ends <- quantile(train$temperature_c, c(0.05, 0.95), na.rm = TRUE) temperature <- map(seq(ends[1], ends[2], length.out = 40), \(level) { swept <- mutate(train, temperature_c = level) tibble(value = level, .pred = mean(predict(forest, swept)$.pred)) }) |> list_rbind() peak <- temperature$value[which.max(temperature$.pred)] # the range of each number input over the training stations ranges <- train |> summarise(across(c(depth_m, temperature_c, chlorophyll_mg_m3, salinity_psu), list(low = \(x) min(x, na.rm = TRUE), high = \(x) max(x, na.rm = TRUE)))) importance |> mutate(rise = round(rise, 3)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|input | rise| |:-----------------|------:| |temperature_c | 0.325| |season | 0.110| |substrate | 0.070| |chlorophyll_mg_m3 | 0.022| |depth_m | 0.020| |salinity_psu | -0.012|
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} rmse = root_mean_squared_error(test["abundance"], forest.predict(test[inputs])) # the rise in test RMSE when an input is shuffled, as in Feature importance shuffled = permutation_importance( forest, test[inputs], test["abundance"], n_repeats=20, random_state=123, scoring="neg_root_mean_squared_error") importance = (pd.Series(shuffled.importances_mean, index=inputs) .sort_values(ascending=False)) # the partial dependence on temperature, as in Partial effects curve = partial_dependence(forest, train[inputs], ["temperature_c"], percentiles=(0.05, 0.95), grid_resolution=40) peak = curve["grid_values"][0][curve["average"][0].argmax()] low, high = train[numeric].min(), train[numeric].max() top = ", ".join(importance.index[:3]) print(f"""Model: random forest of 500 trees, scikit-learn Data: {len(survey)} stations at {sites.nunique()} sites, \ {survey['survey_year'].min()}-{survey['survey_year'].max()} Score: RMSE {rmse:.2f} animals on {test['site_id'].nunique()} held-out sites Relies on: {top}; predictions peak at {peak:.1f} °C Holds for: depth {low['depth_m']:.0f}-{high['depth_m']:.0f} m, \ temperature {low['temperature_c']:.1f}-{high['temperature_c']:.1f} °C""") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> Model: random forest of 500 trees, scikit-learn #> Data: 800 stations at 160 sites, 2018-2023 #> Score: RMSE 4.74 animals on 40 held-out sites #> Relies on: chlorophyll_mg_m3, temperature_c, depth_m; predictions peak at 7.8 °C #> Holds for: depth 5-183 m, temperature 1.9-16.0 °C ``` ::: ::: ::: The card below is written in the page's text with inline code, so each number is the one the chunk above gives: | Entry | The forest on the coastal survey | | ------- | ---------------------------------------- | | **Model** | A random forest of 500 trees, fitted with ranger 0.18.0 in R 4.6.1, with ranger's default settings and seed 123. | | **Intended use** | Predicting the count of the species at stations on this coast, to plan where to sample. Not for water outside the ranges below, other coasts, or saying why the count changes. | | **Data** | 800 stations at 160 sites, surveyed by RV Kaiyo and RV Tsubasa from 2018 to 2023, cleaned in code from the raw file. Fitted to 120 sites (598 stations) and scored on the other 40 (202 stations), held out whole. | | **Inputs** | Depth, temperature, chlorophyll, salinity, substrate and season. Chlorophyll is missing at 6% of stations; gaps are filled with the training stations' median. | | **Score** | An RMSE of 3.96 animals on the held-out sites: a typical miss of about 4 animals at a station. | | **What it relies on** | Shuffling temperature, season and substrate raised the error most. The predictions peak at 7.7 °C and fall in colder and warmer water. | | **Where it holds** | Depths of 5–195 m, temperatures of 1.9–16.0 °C, salinities of 32.7–35.0, in spring, summer, autumn and winter, on gravel, mud, rock and sand. | | **Limits** | The predictions describe how the count varied between the stations sampled, not what causes it. The counts are what the gear caught, so animals the gear misses are missing from the model too. | The Python tab prints the same entries from its own split. When the data or the code change, the card changes with them, and it cannot quote a score the model no longer reaches. ## A card's sentences stay within what the model showed Each sentence of a card or a report is a **claim**: it puts a result into words, and a reader takes the words away, not the numbers. A good claim says what was found and how far it reaches. Three sentences are often written about a model like this one, and the card supports none of them as they stand: - **"Temperature drives the count."** The forest predicts the most animals near 7.7 °C, across the stations as they were found. Warm stations differ from cold ones in more than temperature, and a cause needs an experiment or knowledge of the species. The card says the predictions *peak* there. - **"Warming will reduce the count."** Water warmer than 16.0 °C is outside every station the forest was fitted to, and the card's *Where it holds* entry ends there. - **"Salinity has no effect."** Shuffling salinity did not raise the error (its rise was -0.01 animals), so the forest does not rely on it, with these other inputs beside it. As [Feature importance](feature-importance.qmd) showed, an input that carries the same information as another scores low; it does not show that the input has no effect. Importance scores, partial dependence, SHAP values and surrogates all describe the model. A claim about the species goes only as far as the model's data reach, and the card writes that reach down. ## Key points ::: {.key-points} - An analysis is **reproducible** when the same data and the same code give the same numbers. Keep the raw data, every step in code, a seed above each random draw and the software versions. - A **seed** fixes where the random numbers start, not which step gets which. Here one hidden draw left only 23 of the 40 test sites in place. Set the seed on the line above the draw, or give each function its own `random_state`. - A **model card** travels with a model: what it is, what it is for, its data and inputs, its score on new sites, what it relies on, where it holds and its limits. - Written from the code, the card's numbers cannot drift from the analysis: here an RMSE of 3.96 animals, a temperature peak at 7.7 °C, and depths of 5–195 m. - A **claim** stays within the card: a peak in the predictions, not a cause; the surveyed range, not warmer water; a low score, not no effect. ::: ## Try it yourself 1. In the hidden-draw chunk, move the `recipe()` line above the second `set.seed()`. Do the two runs now share all their test sites? 2. Write the card for the GAM of [Interpretable models and surrogates](interpretable-models.qmd). Which entries change, and what can its *What it relies on* entry say that the forest's cannot?
